references.text: The parallel text in [ref:Matt 27:11|Matthew 27:11] recounts the same scene where Pilate asks Jesus, "Are you the king of the Jews?" and Jesus answers, "You say so". Matthew's version is almost word-for-word identical to Luke's account.

In [ref:Mark 15:2|Mark 15:2], Pilate asks Jesus the same question: "Are you the king of the Jews?", and Jesus gives the same answer: "You say so". This is Mark's parallel account of the hearing before Pilate.

In [ref:Joh 18:33-37|John 18:33-37], John provides an expanded version of Pilate's interrogation, where Jesus explains that his kingdom is not of this world. Pilate asks, "So you are a king then?", and Jesus confirms it, but elaborates on what his kingship entails.

In [ref:1 Tim 6:13|1 Timothy 6:13], Paul points out that Jesus Christ made the good confession before Pontius Pilate. This confession refers precisely to Jesus' testimony of being king, as seen in the hearing in Luke 23:3.

Later in [ref:Luk 23:37-38|Luke 23:37-38], the title "king of the Jews" is used again, both by the soldiers mocking Jesus and in the inscription above the cross. This directly links back to Pilate's question in verse 3.

In [ref:Joh 19:19-22|John 19:19-22], Pilate writes the inscription "Jesus of Nazareth, king of the Jews" and refuses to change it. This shows that Pilate maintained the designation he first questioned during the hearing.

In [ref:Luk 22:67-70|Luke 22:67-70], the Council asks Jesus if he is the Messiah and the Son of God. Jesus' answer, "You say that I am", has the same form as the answer he gives Pilate in 23:3 – "You say so" – and forms the basis for the charges brought forward to Pilate.

The prophecy in [ref:Jes 9:6-7|Isaiah 9:6-7] about the child who will be an eternal king on David's throne forms the messianic foundation for the title "king of the Jews" that Pilate uses in his question to Jesus.
